item.title: Multiple People Are Dead in Erie, Pa., Shooting, City Officials Say
item.description:
Multiple people were killed in a shooting in Erie, Pa., on Friday, according to city officials. The number of those killed or injured was not immediately available.

The shooter was also dead, according to a statement released on Friday night by the mayor’s office, which added that there was “no ongoing threat or danger to the public at this time.”

“This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered,” Chief Rick Lorah of the Erie Police Department told reporters on Friday night, according to WABC-TV in New York. “The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing.”

The identities of the shooter and the victims were not immediately released, and no motive was announced. The shooting took place near 7th and Perry Streets, according to the mayor’s statement. The area around the intersection is mainly residential, according to map images.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Tim Arango and Jonathan Wolfe contributed reporting.

item.title: Christa Pike Discharged From Hospital After Surviving Execution Attempt
item.description:
Christa Pike has been discharged from a Nashville hospital, her lawyers said on Saturday, 10 days after she survived an attempt at lethal injection.

She is back at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, the primary prison for women in Tennessee, her lawyers said. As of Thursday, Ms. Pike had been walking with assistance, but still struggling with concentration and memory.

“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” her lawyers said in a statement. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”

Ms. Pike had spent three decades in the prison, largely in isolation, for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, 19, a classmate in Knoxville. On Sept. 30, she survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital, the second time this year Tennessee has failed to carry out an execution.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: More Than 500 Trees to Be Cut Down at D.C. Golf Course That Trump Wants to Redo
item.description:
The National Park Service will begin cutting down more than 500 trees on Saturday at a public golf course in Washington, D.C., that President Trump is planning to replace with a “championship-level” course.

In a court filing on Friday, Kevin Griess, the superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, said the agency planned to cull hundreds of the trees on the course as part of the clearing operation. The work, scheduled to begin on Saturday, will start at a heavily overgrown area that he said is known as “Trash Island” near the center of the course. He said such work would take place whether or not Mr. Trump moved forward with his plan for an elite golf course at the site.

“In total, the N.P.S. estimates that up to 529 trees that do not contribute to the historic landscape will be removed as part of this tree management and cultural landscape rehabilitation project,” Mr. Griess wrote. “No healthy trees that are contributing features of the historical golf course (such as healthy, historic cherry trees) will be removed as part of this project.”

Facing a federal lawsuit over the proposed golf course renovation, the Trump administration notified a federal judge about the tree-clearing operation because the court requested updates if the administration planned to “conduct any imminent, significant construction or destructive activities of an irretrievable character at East Potomac Golf Course.”

Mr. Griess said the work was being done now because the Park Service had received a “temporary work force support consisting of approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities” to remove the trees.

The D.C. Preservation League filed a federal lawsuit over Mr. Trump’s plans to overhaul the golf course. The Trump administration denied in court that any plans were underway to break ground on the new course by Sept. 1, as Mr. Trump had promised in a post on Truth Social in June. The judge, Ana Reyes, has warned that she would intervene if plans were set in motion without the administration notifying her.

Historic preservationists say the latest tree-clearing work on the course goes beyond merely chopping down dying or damaged trees, and should trigger a new round of public input and reviews under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. The section requires that federal agencies take into account the effects of their actions on historic or cultural properties.

“The work is not routine maintenance, and therefore, for a designated property, they need to undertake Section 106,” Charles A. Birnbaum, president of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, said Saturday.

A top fund-raiser for Mr. Trump has been soliciting donors for the new golf course and a nearby National Garden of American Heroes that Mr. Trump is planning. The project will convert the existing 36-hole property into one that includes a larger 18-hole course that could host major tournaments.

Another of Mr. Trump’s major construction projects is already affecting the public golf course. Soil and debris from the East Wing demolition have been dumped on the site.

item.title: One Officer Killed, Another Shot 12 Times in Philadelphia Ambush
item.description:
One police officer was killed and another was badly wounded early Saturday, when a man ambushed them on the porch of a house in West Philadelphia, police officials said. The suspect, who continued to fire at police as more officers responded to the scene, was eventually captured and taken into custody.

The officer who was killed, Shane Seiber, 40, leaves a 7-year-old son and a 3-year-old daughter, Kevin J. Bethel, the Philadelphia police commissioner, told reporters in a briefing. He was on the force for 10 years.

“He fought valiantly, but he lost his life today,” Mr. Bethel said. “His wife was able to be at his side before he passed, as well as his family.”

The other officer, who has not been named, was shot 12 times. He is in stable condition at Penn Presbyterian Medical Center, Mr. Bethel said. He is 33 years old and a father of five.

In a news briefing early Saturday, Mr. Bethel said that authorities received a call at 12:22 a.m. that a man with a gun was on the porch of a house in West Philadelphia. The two officers were dispatched and arrived at the location a little more than 30 minutes later. When the officers stepped onto the porch, they took “significant fire,” Mr. Bethel said.

As the two were taken to the hospital, police officers and members of the SWAT team were sent to the scene. The suspect, who has not been named, continued to fire at police but was eventually captured after he climbed up a tree. Police recovered a shotgun and two handguns, one of which the man had taken from one of the officers who had been shot on the porch.

“I am so damn proud of the men and women who serve in this department,” Mr. Bethel said, his voice shaking. “Consistently, they go into danger, and they give their lives for this job.”

Over the course of the morning, scores of Philadelphia police officers, firefighters and other emergency workers lined up outside the hospital in a show of respect.

City, state and federal officials expressed their grief.

In a statement, Cherelle Parker, the mayor of Philadelphia, said the city was grieving with Officer Seiber’s family. Senator John Fetterman said the shooting was “a stark reminder of the dangerous job our law enforcement has in keeping us all safe.”

In a post on social media, Gov. Josh Shapiro said that he was ordering flags across Pennsylvania to be flown at half-staff.

item.title: Were Isaias Forecasts Accurate?
item.description:
While Isaias had briefly strengthened into a Category 3 hurricane, it weakened to Category 2 by the time it made landfall on Friday evening in Destin, Fla., with winds up to 105 miles per hour.

Since then, as is typical for hurricanes after landfall, Isaias has been downgraded multiple times. By early Saturday morning, it had dropped to a post-tropical cyclone with winds of 65 m.p.h., according to the National Weather Service.

Still, the hurricane caused pain. Four people were killed in storm-related accidents across Florida and Alabama, officials said.

On social media, however, some have questioned whether the initial forecasts were off, posting videos from home showing relatively minor damage and minimal impacts.

Arinton Mercado, 39, saw things differently.

Driving his truck around Pensacola, Fla., Mr. Mercado said he saw downed trees, fences and power lines, as well as homes with missing roofs and blown-in doors. Mr. Mercado, who works for a home-remodeling contractor, was towing a trailer to help a friend whose home had been damaged.

“We are about to be swamped Monday with calls,” he said.

Around 600,000 customers remained without electricity in Alabama, Florida and Georgia as of early Saturday afternoon, down from about 900,000 in the morning, according to the tracking site PowerOutage.com.

In Destin, where the National Weather Service had initially warned of storm surge between six and nine feet, a gauge on Saturday measured closer to four feet, said Jason Beaman, the meteorologist in charge at the National Weather Service office in Mobile, Ala., which covers the western Florida Panhandle.

“The storm surge for our area was not as high as forecast, and that was simply because the track of the storm moved more over into the Destin area, which gave most of our area an offshore wind,” he said. The surge damage was still being assessed, but Mr. Beaman noted that his team had “seen significant wind impacts from the storm.”

Mr. Beaman said that he felt the National Hurricane Center’s forecasts were “very good,” adding that the minor shifts were “completely normal in a tropical event.”

“They were forecasting just below major hurricane intensity before landfall, and it got to a low-end Category 3,” Mr. Beaman said. “So you’re only talking about 10 miles per hour worth of difference in the intensity forecast.”

He also cautioned that those who had been missed by the storm should not be lulled into a false sense of security. A longtime Gulf Coast resident, Mr. Beaman empathized with the stressful, costly and time-consuming effort that is preparing for a storm that may ultimately not come one’s way.

“For those in areas that did not get the worst impacts, hopefully they feel thankful, but hopefully they still feel encouraged to prepare for the next one, because the next one may not go easy for them,” Mr. Beaman said.

Judson Jones and Amy Graff contributed research.

item.title: Trump Says He Should Have Won 8 Nobels After Being Snubbed for the Prize
item.description:
President Trump returned to a familiar line of attack on Friday morning and Saturday night, castigating the Norwegian Nobel Committee for awarding the 2026 Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer and international judge.

Mr. Trump, who has openly campaigned for the honor to be bestowed on himself, made his case in a nearly 600-word Truth Social post at 11:39 p.m. on Friday, arguing that he had settled eight wars and “should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1.”

He called the decision “an indelible stain on Norway.”

Hours earlier, he shared a post describing Ms. Pillay as “an unabashed hater of America and Israel.”

By Saturday morning, Mr. Trump condensed his grievances into a single paragraph, in which he listed the wars he said he settled; the return of the Israeli hostages; the capture of Venezuela’s former leader, Nicolás Maduro; and the halting of Iran’s nuclear program before concluding: “Yet, with all of that I, or the United States of America, did not get the Noble Peace Prize. WOW!” he wrote.

However, several of the wars that Mr. Trump cited remain unresolved, including those between Israel and Hamas and between Israel and Iran. Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, for instance, recently bristled at Mr. Trump’s claim that he settled conflict between India and Pakistan, saying the United States was not involved in their cease-fire.

The prize has become a recurring touchstone for how Mr. Trump sees his foreign-policy legacy. This year, the committee’s choice drew a sharp contrast with his administration’s approach to international conflict and institutions. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on Saturday.

In its announcement on Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said it was honoring Ms. Pillay for her efforts to uphold a system of international law that is increasingly under attack.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law — national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts nonviolently,” the committee said.

Ms. Pillay served as a judge in her home country and on international courts investigating war crimes, and later as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She also led a United Nations panel that concluded that the Israeli government had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding Israel has rejected.

The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on judges of the International Criminal Court, where Ms. Pillay once served. Ms. Pillay is not under U.S. sanctions.

Last year’s winner, María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, responded to Mr. Trump’s wish to have the award by presenting him with her medal in January. He later called it “a wonderful gesture of mutual respect.”

For her part, Ms. Pillay learned of the award while attending the Nuremberg Forum, an international law gathering in Germany.

While addressing an applauding crowd, she offered a nod to the president’s long pursuit of the prize: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

item.title: 4 Killed as a Weakened Isaias Pushes Through the Southeast
item.description:
At least four people were killed, and hundreds of thousands of others lost power after Hurricane Isaias struck the Florida Panhandle late Friday night and raced into Alabama.

Two people died when trees fell onto homes in Escambia County, Fla., which includes Pensacola, and Birmingham, Ala., according to local officials. A man in Florida was found dead in his garage with a generator running, according to Gov. Ron DeSantis, indicating he might have died from carbon monoxide poisoning. A person in southeast Alabama died after a motor vehicle crash involving fallen trees in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson, a spokesman with the Alabama Emergency Management Agency.

Towns across the region suffered damage, and downed trees and power lines made some roads impassable.

But many residents of the Panhandle, which was hit with winds surpassing 100 miles per hour, were relieved when they ventured outside on Saturday morning.

Trees and fences had been toppled. Signs for restaurants and mini-golf courses had been knocked over, as had some R.V.s. Winds had crumpled garage doors and peeled away the siding and roofs on some homes.

The damage was bad, but nowhere near as catastrophic as many people had feared. Coastal flooding was less intense than had been predicted. “We got away with murder,” said David Gates, 60, who was out walking in Fort Walton Beach.

The hurricane made landfall in Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm, and was the first to hit the mainland United States in two years. It was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone soon after midnight, but it was still bringing heavy rain to much of the Southeast on Saturday as it moved inland, churning along an expected track north through Alabama, Tennessee and Kentucky. Officials in the Carolinas warned residents there to prepare for possible flash flooding. The remnants of the storm will bring rain to the Northeast on Sunday and Monday.

Nearly 900,000 customers lost power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, though about 200,000 had it restored by Saturday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.us, a tracking site.

Officials in Florida said on Saturday that they had not received reports of missing people. “We have not yet received any requests for search and rescue deployment, and I think that is an optimistic sign,” Mr. DeSantis said at a news conference.

The Atlantic hurricane season has been quiet this year; the last time that the first hurricane formed this late in the season was 1905. A major reason for the lull is the El Niño weather system, which typically suppresses hurricanes in the Atlantic, while feeding them in the Eastern Pacific.

On Saturday, two storms, Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel, were headed toward Mexico and the American Southwest, bringing risks of flooding but also potential relief from a brutal Southern California heat wave.

Before Isaias, the last hurricane to hit the mainland United States was Milton, which made landfall in Florida in 2024.

In the Panhandle town of Mary Esther, Maria Hernandez, 75, and her son, Louis Hernandez, 59, said they had ridden out the hurricane in their weather-beaten house, which was built in 1968. A transformer exploded across the street during the storm, spooking their dogs, they said. A tree had blown down in the wind but missed the house. A feared storm surge that might have caused flooding never materialized.

“It’s gone through a lot of hurricanes,” Ms. Hernandez said of the house. “Thank God it’s still standing.”

Her son added that he intended to celebrate by collecting seashells at a nearby beach. “The best time to find them is after a hurricane,” he said.

Reporting was contributed by Amy Graff, Isabella Kwai, Judson Jones, Maia Spoto and Eduardo Medina.

item.title: 5 Killed in Murder-Suicide at a Home in Georgia
item.description:
Five people were fatally shot in a murder-suicide involving family members who lived together at a house in south-central Georgia, the authorities said Saturday.

The shooting was related to domestic violence, officials said at a news conference. The identities of the victims were not released and the police did not provide details about who might have carried out the shooting, which took place Friday night in Douglas, Ga.

Chief Brannen Pruette of the Douglas Police Department said that a few hours before the shooting, a woman — whom he referred to as “the wife, the female victim,” — called to complain about her husband who had been smoking in the house on Robin Lane.

She said “he was killing her with the smoke,” Chief Pruette said.

When officers responded to reports of shots fired at the house, they found four adults dead inside, and a fifth adult wounded. That person was taken to a hospital and later pronounced dead, officials said. While the police said whoever carried out the shooting was dead, it was not clear whether it was one person or multiple people who opened fire.

Chief Pruette said there was no threat to the public associated with the shooting. Aside from noting that the killings were related to domestic violence, he did not offer details about a possible motive.

The shocking burst of violence in Douglas, a small community of about 12,000 roughly 200 miles southeast of Atlanta, left investigators and city leaders searching for answers.

“This devastating loss of life has shaken our community and left families, friends and loved ones facing unimaginable grief,” Mayor Tony Paulk said at the news conference. He added, “No words can adequately express the sorrow surrounding such a tragedy.”

Chief Pruette said the victims’ bodies would be taken to the Georgia Bureau of Investigations crime lab for autopsies.

A similar shooting occurred elsewhere in the country on Friday night. In Erie, Pa., eight people were killed in a residential area, and a shooter was found dead, officials said.

item.title: Some Republicans Reject Trump’s Move to Import Diesel Fuel From Russia
item.description:
President Trump’s announcement of a deal with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to import Russian diesel has drawn criticism from some Republicans running in the most competitive midterm races, as the party grasps for ways to contain soaring energy prices.

The president announced the arrangement, which undercuts U.S. sanctions on Moscow, under pressure to rein in the surging price of diesel. The product’s cost has climbed because of the war with Iran, which has clogged a vital oil-shipping corridor, and high energy prices have become a severe campaign liability for Republican candidates in the midterms.

But the campaigns of two Republicans running in pivotal Senate races — former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan and Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska — expressed disapproval of the deal with Russia. And other Republicans running in competitive Senate and House races had little to say about the agreement, which Mr. Trump trumpeted Friday on social media as a “very big and important” deal, claiming it would swiftly bring down energy costs.

“It’s a grave error by the president,” said Representative Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican from a battleground district who is not running for re-election. “People realize that the sanctions on Russia are appropriate when Russia’s invading a country and bombing cities at night.”

Mr. Bacon predicted the deal would have little effect on soaring diesel prices but would offer a victory for one of America’s adversaries. And the congressman said that the agreement would not help Republican candidates. “It looks desperate,” he said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The deal received some Republican praise. Representative Anna Paulina Luna, a Florida Republican running in a competitive race, wrote on social media that it would “massively benefit the American people.”

The United States introduced sanctions on energy exports from Russia after the country started its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Mr. Trump’s deal, and his declaration Saturday that Ukraine should “get a new president,” escalated U.S. tensions with Kyiv. The issue of U.S. support for the country has for years divided Republicans; the two Republican Senate candidates who questioned the deal have long been supporters of Ukraine.

Some Midwestern Republicans have called for a pause on diesel exports to try to lower costs for American consumers, a notion that Mr. Trump has ruled out.

Energy experts say the deal is not likely to have a major impact on the cost of diesel, which has spiked to around $6.28 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club, up from $3.67 a year ago. Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, an energy consulting firm in Houston, said the deal would introduce a “very small” amount of diesel into the market “compared to U.S. demand.”

In Michigan, Mr. Rogers, who has recently sought distance from Mr. Trump by calling for the president to end both the Iran war and his tariff fight with Canada, told reporters on Friday that he supported an agricultural rebate for diesel, but not the president’s approach.

Mr. Rogers, long a foreign policy hawk, cited concern about offering Mr. Putin a victory. “You just don’t want to give that guy an inch,” he said.

In Alaska, a spokesman for Mr. Sullivan, Nate Adams, said in a statement that the senator “believes American energy dominance is the answer to high prices, and that means producing more of it in Alaska, for Alaskans, by Alaskans, not importing it from Russia.”

Democrats pounced on the deal. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader, wrote on social media that the president had made a “deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes.”

Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee in the competitive Senate race in New Hampshire, said in a statement that the agreement was a “slap in the face to Ukraine and our allies overseas.” The campaign of his Republican opponent, former Senator John E. Sununu, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The high cost of diesel poses a particular risk for Republicans running in states whose farming-heavy economies are powered by diesel, such as Nebraska, Iowa and Kansas.

The campaigns of the Republican Senate candidates in two of those states, Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the president’s deal with Russia. Their hotly contested races, staged in conservative states, could help decide control of the Senate.

Mr. Rogers, Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Hinson have all called for the United States to pause diesel exports. Last month, Mr. Trump proposed banning or limiting U.S. diesel exports, worrying European countries. But last week, he said, “We are not going to be doing the export ban.”

In Wisconsin, another heavily agricultural state, Representative Derrick Van Orden, a hawkish Republican in a battleground district who has been a forceful supporter of the Iran war, said Saturday that he had no comment on the president’s deal with Mr. Putin.

]]>

item.title: Pentagon Again Increases Number of U.S. Casualties in Iran War
item.description:
The Pentagon has again quietly raised the number of U.S. service members killed and wounded during operations related to the Iran war amid widening criticism over the lack of transparency about the conflict’s human and operational costs.The military now is reporting that 21 U.S. service members have been killed, up from 18, and 865 wounded, up by 98 since August.The changes were posted Friday evening to the Defense Casualty Analysis System website, which offers a detailed breakdown of casualties by branch of service, rank, race and ethnicity.

The cause of the increased casualty numbers is not completely clear, since the hostilities between the United States and Iran have largely been in a lull for many weeks.

“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” Representative Adam Smith, Democrat of Washington, and Representative Chrissy Houlahan, Democrat of Pennsylvania, said in a joint statement on Friday.The two House members had demanded an explanation from the Pentagon after the House Armed Services Committee discovered “a discrepancy in the Pentagon’s reporting of casualty numbers” and brought it to the White House’s attention.

“The failure of Secretary Hegseth to immediately take ownership of the problem also does a grave disservice to the men and women putting their lives on the line in service to our country,” they added.

The Pentagon, under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has deliberately withheld casualty numbers from the public, while also attacking reporters for publishing information on them.

In response to reporting by The Washington Post in September that more U.S. troops had died in support of the Iran war than the Pentagon had acknowledged, Mr. Hegseth took to social media to say, “This is DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE.”

The defense secretary also said The Post is “worse than Iranian state media.”

Mr. Hegseth’s office did not immediately respond to a request on Saturday for comment regarding the updated casualty numbers. The increase was reported earlier on Saturday by The Post.

On July 20, the Pentagon added 100 casualties to the war’s tally without explanation. Three days later, the department lowered the number of troops killed during the war, which Mr. Hegseth calls Operation Epic Fury, from 18 to 14 — claiming the discrepancy was caused by “temporary data disruptions.”

Later that month, the Defense Department took the unusual step of claiming that Operation Epic Fury ended with President Trump’s cease-fire announcement in June, and any further deaths and injuries would be accounted for as part of “overseas operations.”

The new casualty numbers come as the war with Iran continues to drag on. Critics have also said the Pentagon has not fully acknowledged the damage done to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which defense officials recognize may be abandoned rather than repaired.

In early July, U.S. Central Command, which directs military operations across the Middle East, resumed near daily airstrikes against Iran. By July 15, Mr. Trump had declared the cease-fire over and resumed a blockade of Iran’s ports by U.S. warships.

Days later, Iranian ballistic missiles struck a base hosting U.S. forces in Jordan, killing three American service members. By the end of the month, U.S. warplanes attacked more targets inside Iran and expanded the strikes to hit Iranian forces in Iraq as well.

A week ago, the Pentagon hastily evacuated B-1 bombers from an air base in Britain after receiving intelligence that Iran might try to attack them with drones.

And while Mr. Trump has not said whether he would resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, The New York Times reported on Thursday that the U.S. military was preparing options to restart major combat operations against Tehran.

item.title: What to Know About Isaias, the First Atlantic Hurricane of the Season
item.description:
A deluge of rain and heavy winds has battered the Gulf Coast as Isaias toppled trees and knocked out power for hundreds of thousands, leaving at least four people dead.

Isaias was the first Atlantic hurricane during what was otherwise a relatively quiet season. After forming in the Gulf of Mexico, the storm became powerful quickly, reaching Category 3 status at its peak.

It was downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane before it made landfall in the Florida Panhandle, near Destin, on Friday, with winds up to 105 miles per hour. Shortly after, it weakened considerably, and by Saturday afternoon, much of the region was reopening.

But parts of the southeastern United States are still at risk of flash flooding as the storm moves north. And hundreds of thousands were still without electricity across the region.

Crews along the coast were cleaning up debris and surveying the damage, which was bad but not as disastrous as residents and officials had feared. Still, trees smashed into homes and cars. Roads were flooded. Roofs were torn off, awnings were shredded and street signs were dangling.

Here’s what to know about the storm:

Isaias is the first hurricane to strike the mainland United States in two years — the last one was Milton, which hit Florida’s west coast, near Sarasota, in October 2024.

After coming ashore near Destin as a Category 2 hurricane late Friday, Isaias was quickly downgraded, which is typical as a storm moves inland. By Saturday, it weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, with winds up to 35 m.p.h.

As Isaias moves north, it is expected to bring downpours in Georgia and parts of the southern Appalachians. Intense rain is forecast to drench North Carolina’s mountainous west on Saturday night.

The storm also prompted several tornado warnings in eastern Georgia as well as central and southern South Carolina.

By Sunday, the storm is expected to cross the Mid-Atlantic region.

At least four people have died in storm-related accidents in Florida and Georgia, according to state and local officials.

Two people — one in Florida and one in Alabama — were killed when trees smashed onto their homes.

One person in Alabama died after a traffic accident involving fallen trees, according to emergency management officials in the state. And one Florida man died in a garage where a generator was running, possibly from carbon monoxide poisoning, Gov. Ron DeSantis said.

More details about the people who were killed, including their names, have not yet been made public.

The storm was expected to push a swell of ocean water ashore along hundreds of miles of the Gulf Coast, bringing floods to normally dry areas. But the surge wasn’t as high as anticipated in many areas.

Winds dragged water away from the shore in stretches of the area around Mobile, Ala. In Destin, the surge was measured at around four feet, despite initial forecasts of between six and nine feet.

East of Destin is where the water likely surged the most, said Morgan Barry, a senior meteorologist at the National Weather Service office in Mobile, which covers the western Florida Panhandle.

Given the less than disastrous effects so far from Isaias, some people on social media questioned the accuracy of the forecasts leading up to the storm’s landfall. But Jason Beaman, the meteorologist in charge at the office, said that he thought the National Hurricane Center’s forecasts were “very good” and that the minor shifts were normal.

In northwest Florida, winds from the hurricane downed trees, fences, R.V.s, and signs for restaurants and mini-golf courses. The ground was littered with broken branches. An abandoned travel trailer was ripped apart, leaving just a pile of debris.

Still, many residents on Saturday voiced relief after Isaias passed the region, as they inspected the damage and found it to be less catastrophic than they had braced themselves for.

Residents in the region are used to being buffeted by hurricanes, including Sally in 2020. Before Isaias’s arrival, beach towns hunkered down, boarding up restaurants and shuttering windows. The storm spoiled plans for the National Shrimp Festival along the Alabama coast, which normally brings tens of thousands of people to the region’s beaches annually.

In Mary Esther, Fla., Maria Hernandez, 75, and her son, Louis Hernandez, 59, said a tree had blown down during the storm but missed their house. A transformer had exploded across the street, scaring their dogs. But their weather-beaten house, built in 1968, has been through plenty of hurricanes and was still standing.

Mr. Hernandez said he would celebrate by gathering seashells.

“The best time to find them is after a hurricane,” he said.

David Ovalle, Judson Jones, Amy Graff, Nazaneen Ghaffar, Madison Malone Kircher, Rick Rojas, Isabella Kwai, Madaleine Rubin and Eduardo Medina contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: ‘Not Pleasant’ but ‘Necessary’: Support at Trump Rally for Public Execution
item.description:
President Trump’s midterm rally tour through the reddest of red states — Alabama, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas — continued Saturday afternoon with a stop in Tennessee. Mr. Trump spoke in the charming, colonial town of Clarksville, a few miles from the Kentucky border.

The people who turned up to see him all seemed to have heard that the Trump administration planned to hold the first legally sanctioned public execution in this country since 1936.

On Dec. 3, a firing squad is scheduled to execute Nidal Malik Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who gunned down 13 of his fellow soldiers, and injured 32 others, while shouting “Allahu akbar,” at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced this week that Mr. Hasan’s execution would be livestreamed. More than a few Republican lawmakers objected, and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it. The president said on Friday that he “absolutely” approved the plan, though he suggested to reporters on Saturday morning that he still had “a decision” to make on whether to “show it.”

Mr. Trump didn’t talk about any of this at his rally in Clarksville, despite holding forth for more than an hour.

Some people shifted uncomfortably in their seats when asked about it. A few said they loved the idea, while others said they wouldn’t watch. But in conversations with 10 people at the rally, no one said they opposed Mr. Trump’s and Mr. Hegseth’s plan.

“I’ll probably watch it on some livestream or something,” said Ron Pool, a 57-year-old man from Indian Mound, Tenn., who said he does not work because he is disabled.

“You don’t have to watch it unless you want to,” said Melanie Hohman, 53, a vice chair of the Wilson County Republican Party. She was there with her husband, Greg, and their 20-year-old son, Luke.

“It’s legal,” the son said with a shrug. (Mr. Hasan has exhausted his appeals through military courts, but experts say he could have a narrow chance through the civilian legal system.)

These conversations were by no means a representative survey of how Americans at large may feel about the return of public execution. But it was a look into how a sample of the president’s most passionate supporters feel about something that many other Republicans have publicly decried as unacceptable in the United States. “Beyond disgusting,” is how Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, put it.

“It’s awesome,” said Myra Ellis, a 63-year-old retired banker from Benton, Ill., who said she plans to watch the execution. “It’s the start of our country getting clean. Anybody that goes onto our military bases and kills our service members deserves to die.”

She was there with her sister, Melissa Reiger, 62, who said she would prefer not to watch. But, she added, “I think for those who want to watch it, hey, I don’t have a problem with that.”

“Maybe I will” watch it, said Paul Paretti, a 63-year-old mechanic. He said he worked at Disneyland in Anaheim for decades before moving to Clarksville.

“Violence isn’t necessarily my thing,” the mechanic added, “but I do think that it’s something that needs to happen in certain situations.”

Mr. Paretti was “really upset” by the botched attempt to execute Christa Pike, the Tennessee woman who lawyers said was discharged from the hospital after surviving what was meant to be a lethal injection. Ms. Pike was convicted of the 1995 torture and murder of a classmate in Knoxville.

Hers was the second failed attempt at lethal injection in the state this year, and it was on the minds of many Tennesseans at the rally. Senator Marsha Blackburn, a Republican who represents the state, spoke before the president arrived. Ms. Blackburn, who is the front-runner to become Tennessee’s next governor, has said that she wants to bring back the electric chair. At the rally, when she reiterated her support for the death penalty, a man in the crowd yelled out.

“Firing squad!!!”

The death penalty is one thing, still debated with passion but legal in 27 states. Livestreaming a public execution is another issue entirely. The Trump administration’s decision to do so will put the country in league with the Taliban, Iran, North Korea and Somalia. Reminded of this in Clarksville, some who said they supported the plan to livestream the execution grew by turns defensive and angry. Others, indifferent. They rejected the notion that by bringing back public spectacles of death, the country’s identity would somehow be changed.

“I wouldn’t compare us to any other country,” said Ms. Hohman, the Republican official from Wilson County. “I mean, we’re the greatest country on earth.”

“I mean, it’s not pleasant, but I think it’s necessary,” said Tracey Aliff, a 57-year-old baker who works at the grocery chain Publix. “I don’t know if I’ll watch it,” she added, “but I think people should have the right to watch it.”

Is it appropriate for children to watch?

“Well, my child is an adult,” she said, “but if I had small children, I don’t think I really would watch with them.”

“One hundred and fifty years ago, they used to hang people on the gallows, and the whole town would come out and look and watch,” said Tim Lincoln, a 68-year-old former member of the military who said he served multiple tours in Iraq. “You don’t think that had some kind of effect on crime?”

“We’re a Christian nation, and that means that we’re not going to let Satan get his way,” he said. Liz Lincoln, a 67-year-old former civil servant, nodded and began to recite scripture from memory: “For with the heart you believe unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation …”

Asked if they planned to watch the execution, she shook her head, and he said, “I’ve seen death. I don’t need to see people die.”

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting.

item.title: A Senator Facing Re-Election Settles a Bakery Bill, 6 Years Later
item.description:
Senator Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, has faced a series of challenges in his unexpectedly close race for re-election.

The latest: A six-year-old unpaid bill for 150 frosted sugar cookies, 100 mini strawberry muffins and 100 fudge brownies, posted online by an angry baker.

The bill, the baker wrote in a social media post that quickly went viral on Thursday, was from Mr. Marshall’s primary night watch party in 2020. The cookies’ buttercream frosting carried his name in blue and yellow. And the source of her frustration was that Mr. Marshall’s 2020 campaign had never paid her the nearly $700 she said it owed her.

On Saturday, Mr. Marshall wrote on social media that he had paid the bill, bringing more attention to a curious saga that his opponent’s campaign had seized on.

The bill began gaining widespread notice on Thursday afternoon, after the baker, Holly Thomas of Hutchinson, Kan., wrote an eight-paragraph Facebook post.

“Six years later, I haven’t forgotten,” she wrote, recalling that repeated phone and email inquires seeking payment had gone unanswered. “That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”

Mr. Marshall, a first-term Republican who may need every vote he can get in a race that polls indicate is neck-and-neck, rushed to respond. He was already contending with a separate revelation about unpaid bills that he had sought to collect on: Last month, The New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, and that he had routinely charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate.

On Thursday evening, Tyson Brody, a spokesman for the Rev. Adam Hamilton, Mr. Marshall’s Democratic opponent, amplified the baker’s post, writing on social media that the bakery bill was “larger than debts for which Roger Marshall had patients sued.” (The unpaid medical bills ranged from $101 to several thousand dollars.)

By Friday, Mr. Marshall had paid Ms. Thomas back, she said in an interview. On Saturday, he addressed the issue in a post on his official X account.

“As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill,” Mr. Marshall wrote. “We have absolutely no idea how this happened.”

But, he added, “as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double.”

The senator attached an invoice showing that he had sent $1,300 to Ms. Thomas’s bakery, Holly’s Sweet Treats. That amount was not quite double the original bill, which had been for $678.75, according to the copy that Ms. Thomas posted on Facebook this week.

It was not clear if Mr. Marshall’s response would satisfy some of the commenters who had seized on the initial post. One had argued that Mr. Marshall owed Ms. Thomas more than $1,400, accounting for interest.

Mr. Marshall’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for further comment on the bill. Several Republican strategists said that Mr. Marshall had handled an unfortunate situation as well as he could.

Ms. Thomas, for her part, said she still had no intention of voting for Mr. Marshall, though she added that his payment was “the right thing to do.”

“I can’t put all the blame on him,” said Ms. Thomas, 43, recalling that the initial order had been placed by a campaign staff member. “But as a business owner, when my staff messes up, it falls on me as well.”

She has been closely following the Senate race and “impulsively” wrote her post as she complained at work about the years-old order, she recalled.

“I just made a post about Roger Marshall and how he didn’t pay me,” Ms. Thomas said she had declared at work. “We’ll see what happens. Maybe he will pay me.”

By Thursday evening, her phone began pinging with messages as she watched her daughter’s volleyball game. She had a theory, she said, for why the post took off.

“He’s let a lot of people down in the state,” said Ms. Thomas, who declined to share her political affiliation. “And people are frustrated with how things are going.”

Some on social media accused Mr. Marshall of hypocrisy, citing his own business practices.

“I do think he’s a hypocrite,” Lindsey Derr, 43, a Democrat in Hutchinson, Kan., who had already planned to vote against Mr. Marshall, said in a phone conversation. She added, “It makes me very upset.”

Mr. Marshall is trying to avoid becoming the first Republican to lose a Senate race in Kansas since 1932. His campaign says the senator gets results for Kansas. But he has been challenged by steep price increases that the Iran war has inflicted on farmers in the state.

On Saturday, Mr. Hamilton’s campaign issued a statement that attempted to encapsulate the episode in a single word: “Cookiegate.”

Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

item.title: 4 Minors Found Dead in Utah Apartment That Had High Carbon Monoxide Levels
item.description:
Four minors, including a 5-year-old girl and an 11-year-old boy, were among five people found dead on Saturday in a Utah apartment where emergency responders encountered high levels of carbon monoxide, the authorities said.

The five bodies were found in a unit of a triplex apartment in Richmond, Utah, the Cache County Sheriff’s Office said in a news release. Neighbors had entered the apartment after hearing carbon monoxide alarms sounding for an “extended period,” the sheriff’s office said.

The authorities did not identify the victims or give a cause of death. The news release said that a man from an adjoining apartment had been taken to a hospital with possible carbon monoxide exposure.

The sheriff’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday night. Richmond is about 100 miles by road north of Salt Lake City, the state capital.

The Cache County sheriff, Chad Jensen, told KUTV 2News, a local television station, that an investigation was underway and that the victims were related. He added that he did not know if the deaths were accidental or intentional.

“I think the majority of our answers will come when the medical examiner is done doing an examination,” he said.

In addition to the 5-year-old girl and the 11-year-old boy, the victims included a 12-year-old girl, a 16-year-old girl and a 43-year-old man, the police said.

Neighbors heard carbon monoxide alarms sounding in the apartment at about 8 a.m. or 9 a.m. on Saturday, Sheriff Jensen said. A neighbor later found a man dead in the apartment’s garage, and called dispatchers at about 12:15 p.m., he said.

Sheriff Jensen added the alarms were “not very loud,” and that he did not know how long the warnings sounded before the neighbors went to intervene.

Firefighters with the Richmond Fire Department arrived at the triplex, but high levels of carbon monoxide prevented them from going inside, Sheriff Jensen said. The firefighters evacuated the surrounding units, he added.

Carbon monoxide is an odorless and colorless gas emitted by cars and many common household appliances, including furnaces, water heaters, clothes dryers and gas stoves, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Unintentional carbon monoxide poisoning not linked to fires kills more than 400 people per year in the United States, the agency said.

Breathing carbon monoxide is dangerous because the gas builds up in the blood and prevents tissues and organs from receiving oxygen.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
